sections.title: Basic Concept of Modifiers and Parallelism
sections.content: Modifiers are words that provide additional information about a noun, verb, or phrase in a sentence. Parallelism means writing similar ideas in the same grammatical form. This makes the sentence clear and balanced.

sections.title: Parallelism in Lists
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the list in the sentence (often connected by 'and' or 'or'). Step 2: Check whether all items are in the same grammatical form. Step 3: If one item is in a different form, change it to match the others. Example: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and to read' is incorrect because 'to read' is in a different form. Correct: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and reading.'

sections.title: Basic Parallel Structure with and, or, but
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the conjunction (and, or, but). Step 2: Check whether both sides have the same grammatical structure. Step 3: Keep both parts in the same form. Example: 'He is smart and works quickly' has different forms. Better: 'He is smart and quick.'

sections.title: Misplaced Modifiers (only, almost, just, nearly)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the modifier words (only, almost, just, nearly). Step 2: Determine which word the modifier is intended to modify. Step 3: Place the modifier close to that word. Example: 'I only ate two apples' can change the meaning. 'I ate only two apples' means I ate no more than two.

sections.title: Meaning Check Strategy
sections.content: In both parallelism and modifiers, clarity of meaning is important. Read the sentence carefully to check whether the modifier is modifying the correct word and whether all items in a list have the same form.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Using different verb forms in a list. 2. Placing a modifier in the wrong position. 3. Unequal structure on both sides of 'and' or 'or'.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: The rule of parallelism is that similar ideas should be written in the same grammatical form. Modifiers should be placed close to the word they modify. This keeps the meaning of the sentence clear.

tricks.title: List Same Form Rule
tricks.explanation: Keep all words in a list in the same grammatical form.

tricks.title: And/Or Balance Trick
tricks.explanation: Both sides of 'and' or 'or' should have the same structure.

tricks.title: Modifier Near Word Rule
tricks.explanation: Place the modifier near the word it modifies.

tricks.title: Meaning Change Check
tricks.explanation: Changing the position of a modifier can change the meaning.
tricks.example: Only I ate two apples (no one else ate them).

tricks.title: Gerund List Trick
tricks.explanation: If one verb is in -ing form, the others should also be in the same form.

tricks.title: Quick Parallel Scan
tricks.explanation: When you see 'and' or 'or', quickly compare the words on both sides.

tricks.title: Only Placement Trick
tricks.explanation: Place 'only' near the word you want to emphasize.

tricks.title: Simple Balance Rule
tricks.explanation: If the first part is a noun, the second part should also be a noun.
